fields.title: 2 Samuel
fields.subtitle: Shemuel Bet, “The Second Book of Samuel”
fields.description: The reign of David, told with an honesty no ancient court would have allowed. It opens with a lament, “How the warriors have fallen!”, for the king who had hunted him, and follows David from Hebron to Jerusalem, the ark carried into the city as the king dances before the LORD with all his might, and the promise at the heart of the Old Testament: “your throne will stand firm forever.” Then, at the height of his power, Bathsheba and Uriah, Nathan’s word “You are the man!”, and David’s “I have sinned against the LORD”; a family torn apart, Absalom’s rebellion, the king weeping up the Mount of Olives, and the cry “My son Absalom!” It closes with David’s song of deliverance, his last words about a morning without clouds, and an altar on a threshing floor in Jerusalem. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of 2 Samuel about?
qa.answer: The reign of King David. Chapters 1–10 tell of his rise: his lament for Saul and Jonathan, his anointing as king first over Judah and then over all Israel, the capture of Jerusalem, the bringing of the ark into the city, God’s covenant promising him an everlasting dynasty (chapter 7), and his kindness to Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth. Chapters 11–20 tell of his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah, Nathan’s rebuke, and the troubles that followed in his family, above all Absalom’s rebellion. Chapters 21–24 gather further stories, lists of David’s warriors, and two of his poems.

qa.question: Who wrote 2 Samuel, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author, and 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book. 1 Chronicles 29:29 mentions records of the prophets Samuel, Nathan and Gad, and Jewish tradition held that Nathan and Gad completed the work Samuel began. Many scholars think chapters 9–20, with 1 Kings 1–2, once formed a separate account of the succession to David’s throne, written by someone close to the court, and that the whole reached its final form as part of a longer history in the time of the kings or later.

qa.question: What is the Davidic covenant?
qa.answer: God’s promise to David, brought by the prophet Nathan in 2 Samuel 7. David wanted to build a house, a temple, for God; instead God promised to build David a “house”, a dynasty: one of his sons would build the temple, God would be a father to him, and David’s house, kingdom and throne would “stand firm forever” (7:16). The promise became the root of Israel’s hope for a Messiah from David’s line, and the New Testament proclaims Jesus as its fulfilment, the son of David whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32–33; Hebrews 1:5).

qa.question: What happened between David and Bathsheba?
qa.answer: In 2 Samuel 11, while his army was at war, David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his soldiers, and had her brought to him and slept with her. When she became pregnant, he tried to cover it up, and when that failed he arranged for Uriah to be killed in battle, then married her. The prophet Nathan confronted him with a parable and the words “You are the man!” (12:7). David confessed, “I have sinned against the LORD”, and was forgiven, but the child died and violence followed in his family. Psalm 51 is linked by its title to this moment.

qa.question: Why is David called a man after God’s own heart if he sinned so badly?
qa.answer: The phrase comes from 1 Samuel 13:14, before David had been anointed, and is echoed by Paul in Acts 13:22. 2 Samuel does not hide David’s sins; it shows them in detail, along with their consequences. What sets him apart from Saul is not sinlessness but his response when confronted: he confessed without excuse, accepted God’s discipline, and kept trusting God’s mercy (12:13; 24:10, 14). Christians have long found in him an example of repentance and of a heart that, even after failing, turned back to God.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name, and David’s poems, his lament for Saul and Jonathan, his song of deliverance and his last words, are set out line by line. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Your house and your kingdom will be secure forever before you; your throne will stand firm forever.’”

— 2 Samuel 7:16

2 Samuel is the story of David as king. It begins with the news of Saul’s death reaching David in exile, and it ends with David, old and chastened, buying a threshing floor outside Jerusalem and building an altar there to stop a plague. Between those two moments David reaches the height of his power, receives the greatest promise God made to any king of Israel, and then, at the very height, falls into the sins that will shadow the rest of his life.

It is a book of extraordinary honesty. Ancient kings had their victories carved in stone and their failures left out. This book tells of David’s triumphs, his generosity and his faith, and then tells, in unsparing detail, of adultery, murder, a cover-up, a prophet’s rebuke, a family torn apart by rape and revenge, a son’s rebellion and a father’s grief. It does not do this to diminish David. It does it to show what God’s grace and God’s promise look like in the life of a real man.

The shape of the book

1 and 2 Samuel were once one book, and 2 Samuel picks up exactly where the first part ends. It falls into three parts.

  • David’s rise (chapters 1–10). The lament for Saul and Jonathan, David king over Judah at Hebron, the long war with Saul’s house, David king over all Israel, the capture of Jerusalem, the ark brought into the city, God’s covenant with David, his victories, and his kindness to Jonathan’s son.
  • David’s sin and its aftermath (chapters 11–20). Bathsheba and Uriah, Nathan’s rebuke, the death of the child, the violence among David’s sons, Absalom’s rebellion and death, and David’s return to Jerusalem.
  • A closing collection (chapters 21–24). Two stories of national judgement, two lists of David’s warriors, and, at the centre, two poems: David’s song of deliverance and his last words.

The turning point comes almost exactly halfway, in chapter 11, with a sentence that is easy to read past: “But David himself stayed behind in Jerusalem.”

“How the warriors have fallen”

The book opens with a man from Saul’s camp bringing David the news of the king’s death, and Saul’s crown and armband, expecting a reward. He claims to have killed Saul himself. David has him executed for raising his hand against “the LORD’s anointed”. Then he sings a lament:

Saul and Jonathan, loved and delightful in life, were not separated in their death. They were faster than eagles and stronger than lions.

— 2 Samuel 1:23

It is a remarkable song from a man Saul had spent years trying to kill. There is no bitterness in it, no word of Saul’s faults, only grief, and a refrain that has passed into proverb: “How the warriors have fallen!” For Jonathan, David’s grief is personal: “I am in anguish over you, my brother Jonathan.” The new king’s reign begins with mourning for the old one.

King over Judah, then over Israel

David does not seize the throne. He asks the LORD where to go, and is told, “To Hebron.” There the men of Judah anoint him king over their tribe, while Saul’s commander Abner makes Saul’s son Ish-bosheth king over the rest. “The war between Saul’s house and David’s house dragged on for a long time.” It is a sordid, bloody story of shifting loyalties and murders, including Joab’s murder of Abner, which David publicly mourns and cannot control: “these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too harsh for me.”

At last the elders of all Israel come to Hebron and make a covenant with David, and he is anointed king over the whole nation. He takes Jerusalem, the Jebusite fortress no tribe had been able to hold, and makes it his capital, the City of David. The book sums up these years in one sentence: “David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of Armies, was with him.”

The ark comes to Jerusalem

David’s next act is to bring the ark of the covenant, the sign of God’s presence, into his new city. The first attempt ends in disaster. The ark is carried on a new cart, as the Philistines had once sent it, and when the oxen stumble, a man named Uzzah reaches out to steady it, and God strikes him dead. David is angry, and afraid, and leaves the ark in a nearby house for three months. It is a hard story, and readers have found it so. It teaches that the holiness of God is not a thing to be handled carelessly, even with good intentions; the law had said how the ark was to be carried, and it was not on a cart.

The second attempt is a festival. The ark is carried properly, sacrifices are offered, and the king himself leads the procession, “dancing before the LORD with all his might”. His wife Michal, Saul’s daughter, watches from a window and despises him for making a fool of himself in front of servant girls. David’s answer is the answer of a worshipper who has forgotten himself: “It was before the LORD that I danced.”

The house God builds

Chapter 7 is the heart of the book, and one of the most important chapters in the Old Testament. David, settled in his palace of cedar, is troubled that the ark of God still lives in a tent, and resolves to build God a house, a temple. The prophet Nathan approves. But that night the word of the LORD comes to Nathan with a different plan. God has never asked for a house. Instead, “the LORD will make a house for you”:

When your days are complete and you rest with your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, one who will come from your own body, and I will make his kingdom firm. He is the one who will build a house for my name, and I will make the throne of his kingdom firm forever.

— 2 Samuel 7:12–13

The word “house” turns in God’s hand. David wanted to build God a house of cedar; God will build David a house of descendants, a dynasty. The son who builds the temple will have God as his father: “I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me.” When that son does wrong, he will be disciplined, but God’s faithful love will not be taken from him as it was from Saul. And the promise reaches beyond any one son: “your throne will stand firm forever.”

David goes in and sits before the LORD, overwhelmed:

Then King David went in and sat down before the LORD and said, “Lord GOD, who am I, and what is my house, that you have brought me as far as this?

— 2 Samuel 7:18

This promise became the hope of Israel through all the centuries that followed. When the kings failed and the kingdom fell and the throne stood empty, the prophets went on looking for a son of David who would reign for ever. The New Testament begins with that name. Matthew’s first line calls Jesus “the son of David”; the angel tells Mary that God will give her son “the throne of David, his forefather”; and the letter to the Hebrews applies to Jesus the very words of verse 14, “I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to me.”

For Jonathan’s sake

Chapter 9 is a short, lovely story that shows what kind of king David meant to be. Kings of that time made sure no one from the previous dynasty survived. David asks the opposite question: “Is there anyone still left from the house of Saul, so that I can show him faithful love for Jonathan’s sake?” There is: Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, lame in both feet since childhood, living in obscurity. David restores Saul’s land to him and gives him a place at the royal table “like one of the king’s sons.” Mephibosheth calls himself “a dead dog”; David treats him as family. Many readers have seen in the scene a picture of grace.

David and Bathsheba

Then comes chapter 11. In the spring, “at the season when kings set out on campaign”, David sends his army out and stays home. One evening, walking on the palace roof, he sees a woman bathing. She is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, one of his own best soldiers. David sends for her and sleeps with her, and she becomes pregnant.

What follows is a cover-up that grows worse with every step. David calls Uriah home from the front, hoping he will sleep with his wife. Uriah, more loyal than his king, refuses to go home while the ark and the army are in tents. So David sends him back to the battle carrying his own death warrant, a letter telling Joab to put Uriah where the fighting is fiercest and then fall back. Uriah dies. David marries Bathsheba. The chapter ends with one quiet line: “But the thing David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”

“You are the man!”

God sends Nathan the prophet to David, and Nathan tells a story about a rich man who, to feed a guest, took the one little ewe lamb a poor man loved like a daughter. David is furious: the man deserves to die. And Nathan says four words that have rung through history: “You are the man!”

He tells David what God had given him, and what he had taken. And he announces the consequence: “the sword will never depart from your house.” David’s answer is short, and it is the difference between him and Saul:

David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan said to David, “The LORD has taken away your sin. You will not die.

— 2 Samuel 12:13

There are no excuses, no blaming of others, no talk of what the people wanted. David is forgiven, and he still suffers what his sin set in motion. The child dies. The title of Psalm 51, the great psalm of repentance, ties it to this moment, “when the prophet Nathan came to him after he had slept with Bathsheba”. And then, quietly, the book tells of another son, Solomon, whom “The LORD loved”, and whom Nathan names Jedidiah, “loved by the LORD”.

The sword in David’s house

The next chapters show Nathan’s word coming true, and they are painful to read. David’s eldest son Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar. David is “very angry”, but does nothing. Tamar’s brother Absalom waits two years and has Amnon murdered, then flees. After three years in exile he is brought home, through the plea of a wise woman of Tekoa who reminds the king that “God does not take away life; instead he devises ways for the banished one not to remain an outcast from him.”

But reconciliation is half-hearted, and Absalom, handsome and ambitious, sits at the city gate winning over everyone with a grievance: “In this way Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” Then he proclaims himself king at Hebron, and David has to flee his own city. The picture of the king leaving Jerusalem is one of the most moving in the Old Testament: “David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went.” He sends the ark back to the city rather than use it as a charm, saying, “let him deal with me as he sees fit”. When Shimei, a man of Saul’s clan, curses him and throws stones, David will not let his men kill him: “Perhaps the LORD will look on my distress and repay me with good in place of his cursing today.”

Absalom’s rebellion ends in a forest, where his head is caught in the branches of a great tree and Joab kills him, against David’s order to “deal gently with the young man Absalom.” When the news reaches David, the victory means nothing to him:

The king was shaken. He went up to the room over the gate and wept, and as he went, these were his words: “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I could have died in your place, Absalom, my son, my son!”

— 2 Samuel 18:33

It is one of the great cries of grief in all literature. Joab has to shake the king out of it, before he loses the army that has just saved him. David returns to Jerusalem, a king again, but not the king he was.

The closing chapters

The last four chapters step outside the story, and are carefully arranged. At their centre are two poems. The first, in chapter 22, is David’s song of thanksgiving “on the day the LORD rescued him from the power of all his enemies and from the power of Saul”, almost word for word the same as Psalm 18: “The LORD is my cliff, my stronghold, the one who sets me free.” The second, in chapter 23, is introduced as “the final words of David”, a short oracle about the righteous ruler, who “is like the morning light when the sun rises, a morning without clouds”, and about God’s everlasting covenant with David’s house.

Around the poems are lists of David’s mighty warriors, including the story of three who broke through enemy lines to bring him water from the well at Bethlehem, which he would not drink but poured out to the LORD, because “Is it not the blood of men who went at the risk of their lives?”

And the book ends with David taking a census of his fighting men, which the book calls a sin and David himself confesses as one. Readers have noticed that this book says the LORD “stirred David up” to do it, while Chronicles, telling the same story, says Satan did; many have understood the two together as God allowing, for his own purposes, a temptation that David was still responsible for yielding to. A plague follows. David prays that it fall on him and not on the people, “But what have these sheep done?” The plague stops at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, and David buys it, refusing to accept it as a gift: “I will not offer the LORD my God burnt offerings at no cost to myself.” According to Chronicles, that threshing floor became the site of the temple his son would build.

How to read 2 Samuel

Read 2 Samuel with 1 Samuel, as one story, and with the Psalms open beside it, since so many of them carry David’s name and a few tie themselves to events in this book. Notice how the book is built around chapter 7, the promise, and chapter 11, the fall, and how the second half keeps echoing David’s own sin back at him: a son who takes what is not his, a household where lust leads to murder, a man who must leave the city weeping.

The book does not name its author. Chronicles mentions records of the prophets Nathan and Gad, and Jewish tradition held that they completed what Samuel began. Many scholars believe that chapters 9–20, with the opening chapters of 1 Kings, once formed a separate history of the succession to David’s throne, written close to the events by someone who knew the court well. Christians hold a range of views on how the book was composed, while receiving it as Scripture and the story of the covenant with David.

Above all, read it for its two great truths held together: that David was a sinner, whose sin had real and lasting consequences, and that God’s promise to him did not fail. The Bible calls him a man after God’s own heart not because he never fell, but because when he was confronted, he turned back to God.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 2 Samuel are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD” and “Lord GOD.” “The LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. Where the Hebrew joins the word for “master” to the name, as it does again and again in David’s prayer in chapter 7, the translation writes “Lord GOD”. The title older Bibles render “the LORD of hosts” is “the LORD of Armies”.

“Faithful love” and “loyal love.” The Hebrew hesed is “faithful love” in the story of David and Mephibosheth, and “loyal love” in David’s song in chapter 22, as in the Psalms.

“How the warriors have fallen.” The refrain of David’s lament, familiar from older Bibles as “How are the mighty fallen”, is translated “How the warriors have fallen”.

Poetry. David’s lament in chapter 1, his song in chapter 22 and his last words in chapter 23 are printed one line per line, as the poetry they are.

Verse numbers. In chapter 19 the Hebrew verse numbers run one ahead of those in English Bibles, since the Hebrew begins the chapter with David’s cry for Absalom; the references in this introduction follow the English numbering.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 1
fields.body_html:
David hears of Saul’s death

After the death of Saul, when David had come back from defeating the Amalekites, David stayed in Ziklag for two days. On the third day a man arrived from Saul’s camp. His clothes were torn, and there was dirt on his head. When he came to David, he threw himself to the ground and bowed low. David asked him, “Where have you come from?” He answered, “I have escaped from the camp of Israel.” David said to him, “What happened? Please tell me.” He said, “The troops fled from the battle, and many of them fell and died. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too.” Then David said to the young man who had brought the news, “How do you know that Saul is dead, and his son Jonathan?” The young man who was telling him said, “I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, while the chariots and the horsemen were closing in on him. He turned around and saw me, and he called to me. I said, ‘Here I am.’ He asked me, ‘Who are you?’ I answered him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’ He said to me, ‘Please stand over me and put me to death, for agony has taken hold of me, though my life still lingers in me.’ So I stood over him and put him to death, because I knew he could not live once he had fallen. Then I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.” Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him. They mourned and wept and went without food until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan, for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel, since they had fallen by the sword.

David said to the young man who had brought him the news, “Where are you from?” He answered, “I am the son of an outsider who lives among you, an Amalekite.” David said to him, “How is it that you were not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” Then David called one of his young men and said, “Go and strike him down!” So he struck him, and the man died. David said to him, “Your blood is on your own head, for your own mouth has testified against you when you said, ‘I killed the LORD’s anointed.’”

David’s lament for Saul and Jonathan

Then David sang this lament over Saul and his son Jonathan, and he ordered that the people of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow, which is written in the Book of Jashar. “Israel, your splendor lies slain on your heights! How the warriors have fallen! Do not tell it in Gath; do not spread the news through the streets of Ashkelon, or the daughters of the Philistines will rejoice, and the daughters of the uncircumcised will celebrate. Mountains of Gilboa, may there be no dew or rain on you, and no fields that yield offerings, for there the shield of the warriors was defiled, the shield of Saul, no longer rubbed with oil. From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the warriors, the bow of Jonathan never turned back, and the sword of Saul never came home empty. Saul and Jonathan, loved and delightful in life, were not separated in their death. They were faster than eagles and stronger than lions. Daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who dressed you in scarlet and finery, who set gold ornaments on your clothes. How the warriors have fallen in the thick of the battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights. I am in anguish over you, my brother Jonathan; you were a great delight to me. Your love for me was a wonder, beyond the love of women. How the warriors have fallen, and the weapons of war are lost!”

fields.title: 2 Samuel 2
fields.body_html:
David is anointed king over Judah

Some time after this, David inquired of the LORD: “Shall I go up into any of the towns of Judah?” The LORD told him, “Go up.” David asked, “Where should I go?” And he answered, “To Hebron.” So David went up there, and his two wives went with him: Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Abigail, who had been the wife of Nabal of Carmel. David also brought up his men, every one of them with his household, and they made their homes in the towns around Hebron. Then the men of Judah came and anointed David there as king over the house of Judah. David was told, “The men of Jabesh-gilead were the ones who buried Saul.”

David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead to say to them, “May the LORD bless you, because you showed this faithful love to your lord Saul by burying him. Now may the LORD show you faithful love and truth. I too will treat you well, because you have done this. So now be strong and brave, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them.”

Ish-bosheth becomes king over Israel

Meanwhile Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, had taken Saul’s son Ish-bosheth and brought him across to Mahanaim. He made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites and Jezreel, over Ephraim and Benjamin, and over all Israel.

Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned two years. Only the house of Judah followed David. David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah for seven years and six months.

The battle at Gibeon

Abner son of Ner set out from Mahanaim for Gibeon with the men of Ish-bosheth son of Saul. Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s men also went out, and the two forces met at the pool of Gibeon. They sat down across the pool from each other, one group on each side. Then Abner said to Joab, “Let some of the young men get up and hold a contest in front of us.” Joab answered, “Let them get up.” So they got up and went forward one by one as they were counted: twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David’s men. Each man caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his side, and they fell down together. So that place in Gibeon was named Helkath-hazzurim. A very hard battle followed that day, and David’s men defeated Abner and the men of Israel. The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai and Asahel. Asahel was as quick on his feet as a wild gazelle. Asahel went after Abner and kept on his track without turning aside to the right or the left. Abner looked back and called out, “Is that you, Asahel?” “It is,” he answered. Abner said to him, “Turn off to your right or your left. Catch one of the young men and strip him of his gear for yourself.” But Asahel would not stop following him. Abner warned Asahel once more, “Stop chasing me! Why should I have to strike you down? How could I look your brother Joab in the face?” But Asahel refused to turn away. So Abner struck him in the belly with the butt of his spear, and the spear came out through his back. He fell there and died on the spot. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped and stood still. But Joab and Abishai kept up the chase after Abner. As the sun was setting, they reached the hill of Ammah, which faces Giah on the road to the wilderness of Gibeon. The Benjaminites rallied around Abner and formed a single unit, and they held their ground on a hilltop. Abner shouted to Joab, “Must the sword go on killing forever? Do you not see that this will end in bitterness? How long before you order the troops to stop chasing their own brothers?” Joab answered, “As surely as God lives, if you had not spoken up, the troops would not have broken off chasing their brothers until the morning.” Joab sounded the trumpet, and the whole army came to a halt. They gave up the chase after Israel, and the fighting ended. Abner and his men marched all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, went on through the whole Bitron, and came to Mahanaim. When Joab came back from chasing Abner, he gathered all the troops together. Nineteen of David’s men were missing, besides Asahel. But David’s men had struck down men of Benjamin and of Abner’s forces, and 360 of them died. They took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb at Bethlehem. Then Joab and his men marched all night, and day broke as they reached Hebron.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 3
fields.body_html:
The war between Saul’s house and David’s house dragged on for a long time. David grew steadily stronger, while the house of Saul grew steadily weaker.

Sons born to David in Hebron

Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, whose mother was Ahinoam of Jezreel. His second was Chileab, whose mother was Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel. The third was Absalom, whose mother was Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. The fourth was Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith, and the fifth was Shephatiah, whose mother was Abital. The sixth was Ithream, whose mother was Eglah, David’s wife. These sons were born to David in Hebron.

Abner goes over to David

While the war went on between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was steadily building up his own power in the house of Saul. Now Saul had had a concubine named Rizpah daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth said to Abner, “Why have you slept with my father’s concubine?” Abner was furious at Ish-bosheth’s words. “Am I a dog’s head on Judah’s side?” he said. “To this day I have kept faithful love toward the house of your father Saul, toward his brothers and his friends, and I have not let you fall into David’s hands. And now you charge me with wrongdoing over this woman! May God deal with me, Abner, ever so severely if I fail to carry out for David what the LORD promised him on oath, by taking the kingdom from the house of Saul and setting up David’s throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.” Ish-bosheth could not say another word in reply to Abner, because he was afraid of him.

Abner sent messengers to David on his own behalf to say, “Whose land is it? Make your covenant with me, and I will give you my support to bring all Israel over to you.” David replied, “Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I require one thing of you: you will not see my face unless you bring Michal daughter of Saul with you when you come to see me.”

Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul to say, “Give me my wife Michal, whom I won as my bride at the price of a hundred Philistine foreskins.” So Ish-bosheth sent and took her away from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish. Her husband went with her, weeping as he followed behind her as far as Bahurim. There Abner told him, “Go on, go back.” And he went back. Abner had talks with the elders of Israel. He said, “For some time now you have wanted David as your king. Now do it! For the LORD has said of David, ‘Through my servant David I will rescue my people Israel from the power of the Philistines and of all their enemies.’” Abner also spoke with the Benjaminites in person. Then he went to Hebron to tell David in person all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin had agreed to. When Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, David held a feast for Abner and the men with him. Then Abner said to David, “Let me set out now and gather all Israel to my lord the king, so that they can make a covenant with you, and you will rule over all that you desire.” So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace. Just then David’s men and Joab came back from a raid, bringing a great deal of plunder with them. But Abner was no longer with David in Hebron, because David had sent him away and he had gone in peace. When Joab and all the army with him arrived, Joab was told, “Abner son of Ner came to the king, and the king sent him away, and he has gone in peace.” Joab went in to the king. “What have you done?” he said. “Abner came to you! Why did you send him away? Now he has got clean away! You know Abner son of Ner! He came to deceive you, to learn all your movements and find out everything you are doing.” After leaving David, Joab sent messengers to go after Abner, and they fetched him back from the well of Sirah. David knew nothing of this. When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the gateway, as if to speak with him privately. There he stabbed him in the belly, and Abner died, in revenge for the blood of Joab’s brother Asahel. Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, “Before the LORD, I and my kingdom are innocent of the blood of Abner son of Ner for all time. May the guilt come down on Joab’s head and on his father’s whole house! May Joab’s family never be without someone who has a discharge or a serious skin disease, or who holds a spindle, or who falls by the sword, or who lacks food!” So it was that Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner, for he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.

David mourns for Abner

Then David told Joab and all the people who were with him, “Tear your clothes, wrap yourselves in sackcloth, and mourn as you walk ahead of Abner.” And King David himself walked behind the bier. They buried Abner in Hebron, and the king wept aloud at Abner’s grave, and all the people wept too.

The king sang a lament for Abner. He said, “Should Abner have died as a fool dies? Your hands were not tied, your feet were not put in chains of bronze; as one falls before wicked men, so you fell.” And all the people wept over him again. Then all the people came to urge David to eat some food while it was still day. But David took an oath: “May God deal with me ever so severely if I taste bread or any other food before sunset!” All the people took note of it, and it pleased them, just as everything the king did pleased all the people. So all the people and all Israel understood that day that the king had no part in the killing of Abner son of Ner.

Then the king said to his officials, “Do you not realize that a leader and a great man has fallen in Israel today? Today I am weak, even though I am anointed king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too harsh for me. May the LORD repay the one who does evil as his evil deserves!”

fields.title: 2 Samuel 4
fields.body_html:
Ish-bosheth is murdered

When Saul’s son heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost heart, and all Israel was alarmed. Saul’s son had two men who were commanders of raiding bands. One was called Baanah and the other Rechab, and both were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the tribe of Benjamin, since Beeroth also is counted as part of Benjamin. The Beerothites had fled to Gittaim, and they have lived there as outsiders to this day.

(Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was lame in both feet. He was five years old when word about Saul and Jonathan arrived from Jezreel. His nurse took him up and fled, but in her haste to get away he fell and was crippled. His name was Mephibosheth.) Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, went off and reached Ish-bosheth’s house in the heat of the day, while he was taking his midday rest. They came into the inner part of the house as though to fetch wheat, and they stabbed him in the belly. Then Rechab and his brother Baanah escaped. They had entered the house while he lay on his bed in his bedroom, and they struck him down, killed him, and cut off his head. Taking the head with them, they traveled all night by the road through the Arabah. They brought Ish-bosheth’s head to David at Hebron and told the king, “Look, here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, the one who sought your life. This day the LORD has given my lord the king vengeance on Saul and his descendants.”

David punishes the murderers

David replied to Rechab and his brother Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, “As surely as the LORD lives, who has rescued my life from every trouble, when the man who told me, ‘Look, Saul is dead,’ thought he was bringing good news, I seized him and put him to death in Ziklag. That was the reward I gave him for his news, how much more when wicked men have killed an innocent man in his own house on his bed! Now then, shall I not demand his blood from your hands and wipe you from the earth?” Then David gave orders to his young men, and they killed them. They cut off their hands and feet and hung their bodies beside the pool in Hebron. But Ish-bosheth’s head they took and buried in Abner’s tomb at Hebron.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 5
fields.body_html:
David becomes king over all Israel

Then all the tribes of Israel came to David in Hebron. “Look,” they told him, “we are your own bone and flesh. In times past, even while Saul reigned over us, you were the one who led Israel out to battle and brought them back. And the LORD said to you, ‘You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel; you will become ruler over Israel.’” When all the elders of Israel had come to the king in Hebron, King David made a covenant with them there in the presence of the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel.

David takes Jerusalem

David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and his reign lasted forty years. At Hebron he reigned over Judah for seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned over all Israel and Judah for thirty-three years. Then the king and his men marched on Jerusalem, against the Jebusites who lived in that land. They told David, “You will not get in here; even the blind and the lame can fend you off.” By this they meant, “David cannot get in here.” But David captured the stronghold of Zion, which is now the City of David. On that day David said, “Whoever would strike down the Jebusites must go up through the water shaft to reach the lame and the blind, whom David hates.” That is why people say, “The blind and the lame will not come into the house.” David took up residence in the stronghold and named it the City of David. He built up the area all around it, from the Millo inward. David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of Armies, was with him.

Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, with cedar logs, woodworkers and stonemasons, and they built David a palace. Then David knew that the LORD had made him secure as king over Israel, and had raised his kingdom high for the sake of his people Israel.

Sons born to David in Jerusalem

David took further concubines and wives from Jerusalem after he left Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to him. The names of the children born to him in Jerusalem are these: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada and Eliphelet.

David defeats the Philistines

News reached the Philistines that David had been anointed king over Israel, so the whole Philistine force went up to hunt for him. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold. Now the Philistines had come and spread out across the Valley of Rephaim. So David inquired of the LORD, “Am I to go up against the Philistines? Will you hand them over to me?” The LORD answered David, “Go up, for I will certainly hand the Philistines over to you.” So David went to Baal-perazim and defeated them there. He said, “The LORD has burst through my enemies ahead of me, like water breaking through.” That is why that place was named Baal-perazim. The Philistines left their idols behind there, and David and his men carried them off.

Once again the Philistines came up and spread out across the Valley of Rephaim. When David inquired of the LORD, he answered, “Do not go straight up. Go around to their rear and attack them opposite the balsam trees. The moment you hear the sound of marching along the tops of the balsam trees, move fast, for that means the LORD has gone out ahead of you to strike down the Philistine army.” David did exactly what the LORD had commanded him, and he struck the Philistines down all the way from Geba to Gezer.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 6
fields.body_html:
The ark is brought to Jerusalem

David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. Then David and all the people with him set out from Baale-judah to bring the ark of God up from there, the ark which is called by the name, the name of the LORD of Armies, who sits enthroned on the cherubim above it. They placed the ark of God on a new cart and took it away from Abinadab’s house on the hill, while Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drove the new cart. So they brought the cart out of the house of Abinadab on the hill with the ark of God on it, and Ahio was walking in front of the ark. David and the whole house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with every kind of instrument made of cypress wood, with lyres, harps, tambourines, rattles and cymbals. When they arrived at the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand and took hold of the ark of God, for the oxen had stumbled. Then the anger of the LORD blazed against Uzzah, and God struck him down there for his error. He died there beside the ark of God. David was angry because the LORD had burst out against Uzzah, and he named that place Perez-uzzah, a name it still has to this day. David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, “How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?” So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David to be with him. Instead he turned aside and took it to the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite. The ark of the LORD stayed three months at the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite, and the LORD blessed Obed-Edom and his whole household. King David was told, “The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-Edom and everything he has because of the ark of God.” So David went and brought the ark of God up from the house of Obed-Edom to the city of David with rejoicing. When those carrying the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, David sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf. David was dancing before the LORD with all his might, and he was wearing a linen ephod. So David and the whole house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with loud shouts of joy and the sound of the ram’s horn. As the ark of the LORD was coming into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked down from the window. She saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and in her heart she despised him. They carried the ark of the LORD in and set it in its place within the tent David had pitched for it. David then offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he pronounced a blessing on the people in the name of the LORD of Armies. He also handed out food to all the people, the whole crowd of Israel, both men and women: a loaf of bread, a cake of dates and a cake of raisins for each one. Then all the people went home, each to their own house. When David returned home to bless his household, Saul’s daughter Michal came out to meet him. She said, “How the king of Israel has honored himself today! He has uncovered himself today before the eyes of his officials’ servant girls, as shamelessly as some worthless fellow would!” David said to Michal, “It was before the LORD that I danced, before the one who chose me over your father and over all his family and appointed me ruler over Israel, the people of the LORD. I will celebrate before the LORD. I will make myself even more undignified than this, and I will be humble in my own eyes. But by the servant girls you spoke of, by them I will be held in honor.” And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child until the day she died.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 7
fields.body_html:
God’s promise to David

When the king was settled in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his enemies on every side, the king said to Nathan the prophet, “Look, I live in a house of cedar, but the ark of God stays inside a tent.” Nathan said to the king, “Go and do all that you have in mind, for the LORD is with you.”

But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan: “Go and tell my servant David, ‘The LORD says this: Are you the one to build me a house to live in? I have not lived in a house from the day I brought the Israelites up from Egypt until this day. I have been moving from place to place in a tent, in a tabernacle. Wherever I have moved about among all the Israelites, did I ever say a word to any of the tribes of Israel that I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, asking, “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?”‘ Now then, say this to my servant David: ‘The LORD of Armies says this: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people Israel. Wherever you have gone, I have been with you, and I have cut off all your enemies in front of you. Now I will make your name great, like the names of the greatest people on earth. I will appoint a place for my people Israel and plant them there, so that they may live in their own place and not be troubled anymore. Wicked people will no longer oppress them as they did at the beginning, ever since the time I set judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. And the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make a house for you. When your days are complete and you rest with your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, one who will come from your own body, and I will make his kingdom firm. He is the one who will build a house for my name, and I will make the throne of his kingdom firm forever. I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with a rod such as people use, with blows such as human beings give. But my faithful love will not leave him, as I took it away from Saul, whom I removed to make way for you. Your house and your kingdom will be secure forever before you; your throne will stand firm forever.’” Nathan spoke to David in keeping with all these words and all this vision.

David’s prayer

Then King David went in and sat down before the LORD and said, “Lord GOD, who am I, and what is my house, that you have brought me as far as this? And as if this were too little in your sight, Lord GOD, you have also spoken about the house of your servant far into the future. Is this the way human beings deal with one another, Lord GOD? What more can David say to you? You know your servant, Lord GOD. For the sake of your word and as your own heart chose, you have done this great thing and made it known to your servant. That is why you are great, Lord GOD. There is no one like you, and there is no God but you, as all we have heard with our own ears tells us. Who is there like your people Israel, the one nation on earth that God went to redeem as his own people? He made a name for himself and did great and awesome things for them and for your land, driving out nations and their gods before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt. You established your people Israel as your own people forever, and you, LORD, have become their God.

And now, LORD God, the word you have spoken about your servant and about his house, make it stand forever, and do as you have said. Then your name will be great forever, and people will say, ‘The LORD of Armies is God over Israel!’ And your servant David’s house will stand firm before you. For you, LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, have revealed this to your servant: ‘I will build a house for you.’ That is why your servant has found the courage to pray this prayer to you. And now, Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. So now, be willing to bless the house of your servant, so that it may last before you forever. For you, Lord GOD, have spoken, and by your blessing your servant’s house will be blessed forever.”

fields.title: 2 Samuel 8
fields.body_html:
David’s victories

Some time after this, David defeated the Philistines and brought them under his control. He took Metheg-ammah out of the Philistines’ hands. He also defeated Moab. He had the Moabites lie down on the ground and used a cord to measure them off: two lengths of cord were to be put to death and one full length kept alive. So the Moabites became subject to David and brought him tribute. David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when Hadadezer went to restore his control at the Euphrates River. David captured 1,700 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers from him. He hamstrung all the chariot horses but kept enough of them for a hundred chariots. When the Arameans of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 of the Arameans. Then David stationed garrisons in Aram of Damascus. The Arameans became David’s subjects and paid him tribute. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went. David took the gold shields that Hadadezer’s officials had carried, and brought them to Jerusalem. From Betah and Berothai, towns of Hadadezer, King David took a great quantity of bronze.

When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, he sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and congratulate him on fighting against Hadadezer and defeating him, for Hadadezer and Toi had often been at war. Joram brought articles of silver, gold and bronze with him. King David dedicated these also to the LORD, as he had done with the silver and gold taken from all the nations he had brought under his control: from Aram, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines and Amalek, and from the plunder taken from Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah. David made a name for himself when he came back from striking down 18,000 Arameans in the Valley of Salt. He stationed garrisons in Edom, throughout all Edom, and all the Edomites became subject to David. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went. So David reigned over all Israel, and he did what was just and right for all his people. Joab son of Zeruiah was commander of the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder; Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Seraiah was secretary; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David’s sons were priests.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 9
fields.body_html:
David shows faithful love to Mephibosheth

David asked, “Is there anyone still left from the house of Saul, so that I can show him faithful love for Jonathan’s sake?” Now there was a servant of Saul’s house named Ziba, and they summoned him to David. The king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” “I am your servant,” he said. The king asked, “Is there no one left from the house of Saul, to whom I can show the faithful love of God?” Ziba answered the king, “There is still a son of Jonathan. He is lame in both feet.” “Where is he?” the king asked him. Ziba said to the king, “He is in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar.” So King David sent and had him brought out of the house of Machir son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar. Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face and bowed low. David said, “Mephibosheth!” “I am your servant,” he answered. David said to him, “Do not be afraid. I will certainly show you faithful love for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will give you back all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul, and you yourself will always eat at my table.” He bowed down again and said, “Who is your servant, that you would pay attention to a dead dog like me?” Then the king summoned Ziba, Saul’s attendant, and said to him, “I have given your master’s grandson everything that belonged to Saul and to his whole family. You, your sons and your servants are to work the land for him and bring in its harvest, to provide food for your master’s grandson to eat. But Mephibosheth himself, your master’s grandson, will always eat at my table.” Ziba had fifteen sons as well as twenty servants. Ziba said to the king, “Your servant will do everything that my lord the king commands his servant.” So the king said, “Mephibosheth will eat at my table like one of the king’s sons.” Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica. Everyone who lived in Ziba’s household became servants of Mephibosheth. So Mephibosheth made his home in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table. He was lame in both feet.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 10
fields.body_html:
David defeats the Ammonites and the Arameans

Some time after this, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun became king in his place. David said, “I will show faithful love to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed faithful love to me.” So David sent his officials to console Hanun over the death of his father. And David’s officials came to the land of the Ammonites. But the Ammonite officials said to Hanun their lord, “Do you really think David is honoring your father by sending men to comfort you? Has David not sent his officials to you to explore the city, spy it out, and overthrow it?” So Hanun seized David’s officials, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut off their garments in the middle at their buttocks, and sent them away. When David was told, he sent messengers to meet them, because the men were deeply ashamed. The king said, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then come home.” When the Ammonites saw that they had made themselves hateful to David, they sent and hired 20,000 foot soldiers from the Arameans of Beth-rehob and of Zobah, the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and 12,000 men from Tob. When David heard about this, he sent out Joab with the whole army of warriors. The Ammonites marched out and formed their battle line at the gateway of the city, while the Arameans of Zobah and Rehob, along with the men of Tob and Maacah, took a separate position in the open country. Joab saw that the battle lines faced him both in front and behind. So he picked some of Israel’s best troops and lined them up against the Arameans. He put the rest of the troops under the command of his brother Abishai, and he lined them up against the Ammonites. Joab said, “If the Arameans are too strong for me, you must come to my rescue. But if the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come and rescue you. Be strong! Let us show courage for the sake of our people and the cities of our God. And may the LORD do what seems good to him.” Then Joab and the troops with him advanced to fight the Arameans, and the Arameans fled from him. When the Ammonites saw the Arameans flee, they also fled from Abishai and withdrew into the city. Then Joab turned back from fighting the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem. When the Arameans saw that they had been beaten by Israel, they gathered their forces together. Hadadezer sent for the Arameans who were beyond the Euphrates River and brought them out. They came to Helam, and Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, was at their head. When David was told, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam. The Arameans lined up for battle against David and fought with him. But the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed the crews of 700 of their chariots and 40,000 horsemen. He also struck down Shobach, the commander of their army, and he died there. All the kings who were subject to Hadadezer saw that Israel had defeated them, so they made peace with Israel and became its subjects. After this the Arameans were afraid to give the Ammonites any more help.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 11
fields.body_html:
When the year came round again, at the season when kings set out on campaign, David sent out Joab with his officers and the whole army of Israel. They ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David himself stayed behind in Jerusalem.

David and Bathsheba

As evening came on, David got up from where he had been lying and walked back and forth on the roof of the royal palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing, and she was very beautiful to look at. David sent someone to ask about the woman, and the answer came back, “Is that not Bathsheba, Eliam’s daughter, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?” David sent messengers and had her brought. She came to him, and he slept with her; she was purifying herself from her uncleanness. Then she went back to her house. The woman found she had conceived, and she sent to let David know: “I am pregnant.” Then David sent orders to Joab: “Have Uriah the Hittite sent to me.” So Joab sent Uriah to David. When Uriah arrived, David asked him how Joab was, how the troops were, and how the war was going. Then David told Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah left the palace, and a present from the king was carried out after him. Uriah, however, spent the night at the palace door alongside all his lord’s servants. He did not go down to his own house. Word reached David that Uriah had not gone down to his house. So David asked him, “You have just come back from a journey, have you not? Why did you not go down to your house?” Uriah answered David, “The ark and Israel and Judah are living in shelters, and my lord Joab and my lord’s men are camped out in the open country. Am I to go off to my own house, eat and drink, and sleep with my wife? I swear by your life, by your very life, I will not do this!” Then David told Uriah, “Stay here one more day, and tomorrow I will let you go.” So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next. David invited him, and Uriah ate and drank in his presence, and David got him drunk. But in the evening Uriah went out to lie down on his mat among his lord’s servants; he did not go down to his house. Next morning David wrote to Joab and had Uriah carry the letter. In the letter he wrote, “Station Uriah in the front line where the battle is heaviest. Then fall back from him, so that he is struck down and dies.”

Uriah is killed

Joab had the city closely watched, and he posted Uriah at a spot where he knew the enemy had its bravest fighters. The defenders came out of the city and fought Joab’s forces. A number of the troops, David’s men, fell, and Uriah the Hittite died as well. Joab sent a messenger to tell David everything that had happened in the fighting. He gave the messenger these instructions: “When you have finished telling the king the whole story of the battle, and if the king flares up in anger and asks you, ‘Why did you go so close to the city to fight? Did you not know they would shoot down from the wall? Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? Was it not a woman? She let an upper millstone fall on him from the top of the wall, and he died at Thebez. Why did you go near the wall?’ then tell him, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too.’” So the messenger set out, and when he arrived he told David everything Joab had sent him to say. The messenger told David, “The enemy were stronger than we were and came out at us in the open country, but we pushed them back as far as the gate. Then the archers shot at your men from the wall. Some of the king’s men are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too.”

David said to the messenger, “Tell Joab this: ‘Do not let this matter look evil to you. The sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack on the city and tear it down.’ So encourage him.” Word reached Uriah’s wife that her husband Uriah was dead, and she lamented for her husband. Once her time of mourning was over, David sent for her and took her into his household. She became his wife, and she gave birth to a son for him. But the thing David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 12
fields.body_html:
Nathan confronts David

The LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said, “In a certain city there were two men, one of them rich and the other poor. The rich man had a great many sheep and cattle. But the poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb that he had bought. He nurtured it, and it grew up with him alongside his children. It shared his bit of bread, drank from his cup and lay in his arms; it was like a daughter to him. Then a traveler came to the rich man. He did not want to take one of his own sheep or cattle to prepare for the visitor who had come to him. So he took the poor man’s ewe lamb and prepared it for his guest.” David’s anger burned hot against the man. “As surely as the LORD lives,” he said to Nathan, “the man who did this deserves to die! He must pay back four times over for the lamb, because he did this and because he had no pity.” Nathan said to David, “You are the man! The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from Saul’s power. I gave you your master’s house and placed your master’s wives in your embrace. I gave you the house of Israel and Judah too. And had that been too little, I would have given you much more besides. Why have you despised the word of the LORD by doing what is evil in my sight? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife to be your wife. You killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. So now the sword will never depart from your house, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.’

The LORD says this: ‘I am about to raise up disaster against you from within your own household. Before your eyes I will take your wives and give them to one who is close to you, and he will lie with your wives in broad daylight. You acted in secret, but I will do this in front of all Israel, in broad daylight.’”

David admits his sin

David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan said to David, “The LORD has taken away your sin. You will not die. But because by doing this you have given the enemies of the LORD every reason to scorn him, the son who has been born to you will surely die.” After Nathan had gone home, the LORD struck the child whom Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and the boy fell gravely ill. David pleaded with God for the boy. He fasted, and he went in and spent the nights lying on the ground. The elders of his household stood beside him to get him up from the ground, but he refused, and he would not eat any food with them. The child died on the seventh day, and David’s servants were afraid to give him the news. They said, “While the child was still living, we spoke to him and he paid no attention to us. How can we tell him the child is dead? He may do something harmful.” When David saw his servants whispering to one another, he realized that the child was dead. So he asked his servants, “Has the child died?” They answered, “He has died.” Then David got up from the ground. He washed, put oil on himself and changed his clothes. He entered the house of the LORD and bowed in worship. After that he went to his own house and asked for food, and when they set it before him, he ate. His servants said to him, “What is this you have done? While the child was alive, you fasted and wept for him, but now that the child is dead, you get up and eat!” He said, “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept. I thought, ‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let the child live.’ But now he has died. Why should I go on fasting? Am I able to bring him back? I will go to him one day, but he will not come back to me.” Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He went to her and slept with her, and she gave birth to a son, and she named him Solomon. The LORD loved him, and he sent word through Nathan the prophet, and he named him Jedidiah because of the LORD.

Rabbah is captured

Meanwhile Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city. Joab sent messengers to tell David, “I have fought against Rabbah, and I have taken the city’s water supply. Now gather the rest of the troops, camp against the city and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city myself, and it will be named after me.” So David gathered all the troops and went to Rabbah. He fought against it and captured it. He took the crown from their king’s head. It weighed about 75 pounds of gold and held a precious stone, and it was placed on David’s head. He also brought a great amount of plunder out of the city. He brought out the people who were in the city and put them to work with saws, iron picks and iron axes, and he made them labor at the brick molds. He did the same to all the towns of the Ammonites. Then David and all the troops returned to Jerusalem.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 13
fields.body_html:
Amnon and Tamar

Some time after this, Absalom son of David had a beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon son of David fell in love with her. Amnon was so tormented over his sister Tamar that he made himself ill. She was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her. Now Amnon had a friend named Jonadab son of Shimeah, David’s brother. Jonadab was a very shrewd man. He asked him, “Why do you look so worn out, son of the king, morning after morning? Will you not tell me?” Amnon answered him, “I am in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom’s sister.” Jonadab said to him, “Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. Then, when your father comes to visit you, tell him, ‘I beg you, let my sister Tamar come and feed me. Have her prepare the food here in front of me, so that I can watch and then eat it from her hand.’” So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to him, “I beg you, let my sister Tamar come here and make a couple of cakes in front of me, so that I can eat from her hand.” David sent word to Tamar at the palace: “Please go to your brother Amnon’s house and prepare some food for him.” So Tamar went to her brother Amnon’s house, where he was lying in bed. She took dough, kneaded it, made cakes while he watched, and baked them. Then she took the pan and set the cakes out before him, but he refused to eat. “Send everyone out of here,” Amnon said, and they all left him. Amnon then told Tamar, “Bring the food in here to the bedroom, and I will eat from your hand.” So Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom. But when she brought them close for him to eat, he grabbed her and said to her, “Come, lie with me, my sister.” “No, my brother!” she said to him. “Do not violate me! Such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this outrageous thing. As for me, where could I go with my shame? And you would be counted among the outrageous fools in Israel. Now please, speak to the king. He will not keep me from you.” But he would not listen to her. He was stronger than she was, and he violated her and lay with her by force. Then Amnon turned on her with a fierce hatred. What he felt against her now was stronger than the love he had once felt for her. “Get up and go!” Amnon said to her. “No!” she said to him. “Sending me away would be a greater wrong than what you have already done to me.” But he would not listen to her. He called the young man who attended him and said, “Put this woman out of my room, and bolt the door behind her.” She was wearing a long-sleeved robe, the kind of robe the king’s unmarried daughters wore. His servant put her out and bolted the door behind her. Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long-sleeved robe she was wearing. She put her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went. Absalom, her brother, asked her, “Has your brother Amnon been with you? Now, my sister, keep quiet. He is your brother. Do not take this matter to heart.” So Tamar lived in her brother Absalom’s house, a desolate woman. When King David heard about all these things, he was very angry. Absalom said nothing at all to Amnon, good or bad. He hated Amnon because he had violated his sister Tamar.

Absalom kills Amnon

Two full years later, Absalom had sheepshearers at work at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and he invited all the king’s sons. Absalom came to the king and said, “Your servant has sheepshearers at work. Will the king and his officials please come with your servant?” “No, my son,” the king said to Absalom. “We should not all go; we would only be a burden to you.” Absalom pressed him, but he would not go, though he gave him his blessing. Then Absalom said, “If you will not come, then please let my brother Amnon go with us.” The king asked him, “Why should he go with you?” But Absalom kept pressing him, so he let Amnon and all the king’s sons go with him.

Absalom gave his servants these orders: “Watch closely. When Amnon is in high spirits from the wine and I tell you, ‘Strike Amnon,’ then kill him. Do not be afraid. Have I not given you the order myself? Be strong and act like brave men.” So Absalom’s servants did to Amnon exactly what Absalom had ordered. Then all the king’s sons got up, mounted their mules and fled. While they were still on the road, the report reached David: “Absalom has struck down all the king’s sons; not one of them is left!”

The king rose, tore his clothes and lay on the ground. All his officials stood beside him with their clothes torn.

But Jonadab son of Shimeah, David’s brother, spoke up: “My lord should not think they have killed all the young men, the king’s sons. Only Amnon is dead. Absalom has been determined to do this ever since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar. So now, my lord the king should not take to heart the report that all the king’s sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead.”

Absalom flees

Meanwhile Absalom fled. The young man on watch looked up and saw many people coming along the road behind him, down the side of the hill. Jonadab said to the king, “See, the king’s sons are here! It has happened just as your servant said.” He had hardly finished speaking when the king’s sons came in, weeping aloud. The king and all his officials also wept very bitterly. Absalom fled; he went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. David grieved for his son day after day. So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and he stayed there three years. And King David longed to go out to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon’s death.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 14
fields.body_html:
Joab and the woman from Tekoa

Joab son of Zeruiah knew that the king’s heart was set on Absalom. So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought a wise woman from there. He said to her, “Act as though you are in mourning. Put on mourning clothes and do not anoint yourself with oil. Behave like a woman who has been grieving for the dead a long time. Then go to the king and speak to him in this way.” And Joab put the words in her mouth. When the woman of Tekoa addressed the king, she threw herself face down on the ground and bowed low. “Help me, Your Majesty!” she said.

The king asked her, “What is troubling you?” She answered, “Sadly, I am a widow. My husband is dead. Your servant had two sons. The two of them got into a fight out in the field, with no one there to pull them apart, and one struck the other and killed him. Now the whole clan has risen up against your servant. They say, ‘Hand over the man who struck down his brother. We will put him to death to pay for the life of the brother he killed, and so do away with the heir as well.’ So they would put out the one coal I have left, and leave my husband neither name nor survivor on the face of the earth.”

The king said to the woman, “Go home. I will give orders about your case.” The woman of Tekoa replied, “My lord the king, let the guilt be on me and on my father’s house, and let the king and his throne be free of blame.”

The king said, “If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he will never trouble you again.” She said, “Please let the king call on the LORD your God, so that the avenger of blood will not add to the destruction, and my son will not be destroyed.” He said, “As surely as the LORD lives, not one hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.” Then the woman said, “Please let your servant say one more thing to my lord the king.” “Speak,” he said.

The woman said, “Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? By speaking as he has, the king convicts himself, since the king has not brought home his own banished son. We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away life; instead he devises ways for the banished one not to remain an outcast from him. Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people frightened me. Your servant thought, ‘Let me speak to the king. Perhaps the king will grant his servant’s request.’ For the king will listen and rescue his servant from the hand of the one who seeks to destroy both me and my son, cutting us off from the inheritance God has given. Your servant thought, ‘Let what my lord the king says bring me rest, since my lord the king is like an angel of God in telling good from evil.’ May the LORD your God be with you!”

Then the king answered the woman, “Do not hide from me anything I am about to ask you.” “Let my lord the king speak,” the woman said. The king asked, “Has Joab had a hand in all this with you?” The woman replied, “My lord the king, as surely as you live, no one can turn aside to the right or the left from anything my lord the king says. Yes, it was your servant Joab who gave me orders. He put all these words in your servant’s mouth. Your servant Joab did this to change the way things stand. But my lord is as wise as an angel of God, and knows everything that happens in the land.”

Absalom returns to Jerusalem

Then the king said to Joab, “Very well, I will do this. Go and bring back the young man Absalom.” Joab threw himself face down on the ground, bowed low and blessed the king. “Today,” Joab said, “your servant knows that my lord the king looks on me with favor, because the king has granted your servant’s request.” So Joab set out and went to Geshur, and he brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.

But the king said, “He is to go to his own house. He must not come into my presence.” So Absalom went to his own house and did not come into the king’s presence.

In all Israel there was no man so highly praised for his good looks as Absalom; there was not a flaw in him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. Whenever he cut his hair, which he did once a year because it grew heavy on him, he would weigh it, and it came to about 5 pounds by the royal standard. Three sons and one daughter were born to Absalom. His daughter’s name was Tamar, and she was a beautiful woman.

Absalom sees the king again

Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without coming into the king’s presence. Absalom then sent for Joab, meaning to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. He sent a second time, but still Joab would not come. So he told his servants, “You see Joab’s field beside mine, where he has barley growing. Go and set fire to it.” And Absalom’s servants set fire to the field.

Then Joab went straight to Absalom at his house and said, “Why did your servants set fire to my field?” Absalom answered Joab, “I sent word to you to come here, so that I could send you to the king to ask, ‘Why did I come back from Geshur? I would be better off if I were still there.’ Now let me come into the king’s presence. If I am guilty of anything, let him put me to death.” So Joab went to the king and told him, and the king summoned Absalom. Absalom came to the king and bowed down before him with his face to the ground, and the king kissed Absalom.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 15
fields.body_html:
Absalom plots against David

Some time after this, Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, with fifty men to run ahead of him. Absalom would get up early and stand beside the road that led to the city gate. Whenever anyone had a dispute to bring before the king for judgment, Absalom would call out to him, “What town are you from?” And he would answer, “Your servant is from such and such a tribe of Israel.” Absalom would say to him, “Look, your claims are good and right, but there is no one from the king to hear your case.” Absalom would also say, “If only someone would make me judge in the land! Then anyone with a dispute or a case could come to me, and I would see that justice is done.” And whenever anyone approached to bow low before him, Absalom would stretch out his hand, take hold of the man and kiss him. Absalom acted this way toward every Israelite who came to the king for judgment. In this way Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

When forty years had come to an end, Absalom said to the king, “Please let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vow I made to the LORD. For your servant made a vow while I was living at Geshur in Aram. I said, ‘If the LORD really brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the LORD.’” The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he got up and went to Hebron.

Absalom’s revolt and David’s flight

Meanwhile Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel to say, “As soon as you hear the sound of the ram’s horn, say, ‘Absalom has become king in Hebron!’” Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They had been invited as guests and went in all innocence, knowing nothing about the plot. While Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he also sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his town of Giloh. So the conspiracy grew strong, and the number of people supporting Absalom kept increasing. A messenger came to David and said, “The hearts of the men of Israel have gone over to Absalom.” Then David said to all his officials who were with him in Jerusalem, “Get up! We must flee, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Leave at once, or he will move quickly, overtake us, bring disaster on us and put the city to the sword.” The king’s officials said to the king, “Whatever my lord the king decides, your servants are ready.” So the king set out, with all his household following him. But he left ten concubines behind to look after the palace. So the king went out with all the people following him, and they stopped at the last house. All his officials marched past him, with every one of the Cherethites and the Pelethites. And all the Gittites, the six hundred men who had followed him from Gath, marched past the king. Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why should you come with us too? Go back and stay with the king. You are a foreigner, and an exile from your own homeland as well. You came only yesterday. Should I make you wander about with us today, when I do not even know where I am going? Go back, and take your kinsmen with you. May faithful love and faithfulness go with you.” But Ittai replied to the king, “As surely as the LORD lives, and by the life of my lord the king, in whatever place my lord the king may be, whether it means death or life, there your servant will be.” David said to Ittai, “Go ahead, then, and march on.” So Ittai the Gittite marched on with all his men and all the families who were with him. The whole countryside wept aloud as all the people passed by. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people went on toward the road to the wilderness. Zadok was there too, with all the Levites carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set the ark of God down, and Abiathar went up, while the people finished leaving the city. Then the king said to Zadok, “Take the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the sight of the LORD, he will bring me home again and let me see the ark and his dwelling place once more. But if he says, ‘I am not pleased with you,’ then here I am; let him deal with me as he sees fit.”

David sends the priests back

The king also said to Zadok the priest, “Do you understand? Go back to the city in peace, and take your two sons with you: your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar.
