Look, I will wait at the fords in the wilderness until word comes from you to let me know what is happening.” So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there. David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went. His head was covered, and he walked barefoot. All the people with him covered their heads too, and they went up weeping as they climbed. Then David was told, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” And David prayed, “LORD, please turn the advice of Ahithophel into foolishness.” When David reached the summit, where God was worshiped, Hushai the Archite came to meet him there. His robe was torn and there was earth on his head. David told him, “If you go on with me, you will only weigh me down. But if you go back to the city and tell Absalom, ‘O king, I will be your servant. Before, I was your father’s servant, but now I will be yours,’ then you can defeat the advice of Ahithophel for me. Zadok and Abiathar the priests will be there with you, will they not? Tell them everything you hear from the king’s palace. Their two sons are there with them, Zadok’s son Ahimaaz and Abiathar’s son Jonathan. Send them to me with everything you hear.” So Hushai, David’s friend, came into the city just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 16
fields.body_html:
Ziba and Shimei meet David

David had gone a little way past the top of the hill when Ziba, Mephibosheth’s attendant, met him. He had a pair of saddled donkeys loaded with 200 loaves of bread, 100 clusters of raisins, 100 portions of summer fruit and a skin of wine. The king asked Ziba, “What do you mean by these?” Ziba answered, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride on. The bread and the summer fruit are food for the young men, and the wine is for anyone who grows faint in the wilderness.” The king asked, “And where is your master’s grandson?” Ziba answered the king, “He is staying in Jerusalem. He has said, ‘Today the house of Israel will give me back my grandfather’s kingdom.’” Then the king said to Ziba, “Everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours.” Ziba said, “I bow before you. May I find favor with you, my lord the king.” As King David reached Bahurim, a man from the clan of Saul’s family came out from there. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and as he came out he kept cursing. He threw stones at David and at all King David’s officials, even though all the people and all the warriors were on David’s right and on his left. As he cursed, Shimei said, “Get out! Get out, you man of blood, you worthless man! The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of Saul’s family, whose throne you took. The LORD has handed the kingdom over to your son Absalom. And see, disaster has caught you, because you are a man of blood!” Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why let this dead dog curse my lord the king? Please let me cross over and cut off his head.”

But the king said, “What does this have to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse like this, because the LORD has told him, ‘Curse David.’ Who then can ask, ‘Why have you done this?’”

David said to Abishai and to all his officials, “Look, my own son, who came from my own body, is trying to kill me. How much more, then, this Benjaminite! Leave him alone and let him curse, because the LORD has told him to. Perhaps the LORD will look on my distress and repay me with good in place of his cursing today.” So David and his men went on along the road, while Shimei kept pace with him on the hillside across from him, cursing as he went, throwing stones toward him and flinging dust.

The king and all the people with him arrived worn out, and he rested there and recovered his strength. Meanwhile Absalom came to Jerusalem with all the people, the men of Israel, and Ahithophel was with him. When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to him, “Long live the king! Long live the king!” Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this your faithful love for your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?” Hushai answered Absalom, “No! I will belong to the one whom the LORD, this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, and I will stay with him. Besides, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? Just as I served your father, so I will serve you.”

Ahithophel’s advice

Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give us your advice. What should we do?” Ahithophel answered Absalom, “Sleep with your father’s concubines, whom he left to look after the palace. Then all Israel will hear that you have made yourself hateful to your father, and all who are with you will be strengthened.” So they set up the tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom slept with his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel. In those days the advice Ahithophel gave was like asking for a word from God. That is how both David and Absalom regarded all of Ahithophel’s advice.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 17
fields.body_html:
Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me pick out twelve thousand men, and I will set out and go after David tonight. I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged and throw him into a panic. All the people with him will run away, and I will strike down the king alone. Then I will bring all the people back to you. The man you are after is worth the return of them all. All the people will be at peace.” The plan seemed right to Absalom and to all the elders of Israel.

Hushai gives his advice

But Absalom said, “Call Hushai the Archite as well, and let us hear what he has to say too.” When Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, “This is what Ahithophel has proposed. Should we do as he says? If not, tell us what you think.”

Hushai answered Absalom, “This time the advice Ahithophel has given is not good.” Hushai went on, “You know your father and his men. They are warriors, and they are fierce and enraged, like a bear in the wild robbed of her cubs. Your father is an experienced fighter, and he will not spend the night with the troops. Even now he is hiding in one of the caves or in some other place. When some of the troops fall in the first attack, whoever hears of it will say, ‘The troops who follow Absalom have been slaughtered.’ Then even the bravest man, whose heart is like a lion’s, will lose all courage, for all Israel knows that your father is a warrior and that the men with him are brave. So my advice is this: let all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the sand by the sea, and lead them into battle yourself. Then we will come upon him wherever he may be found and settle on him the way dew falls on the ground. Neither he nor any of the men with him will be left, not even one. If he pulls back into a town, all Israel will haul ropes up to it, and we will drag the whole place down into the valley until not even a pebble is left there.”

Then Absalom and all the men of Israel declared, “Hushai the Archite gives better advice than Ahithophel.” For the LORD had decreed that Ahithophel’s good advice would be defeated, so that the LORD could bring disaster on Absalom.

David is warned

Hushai told Zadok and Abiathar the priests, “Ahithophel advised Absalom and the elders of Israel to do this and that, but I advised this and that. Now send word quickly and tell David, ‘Do not camp tonight in the plains by the wilderness. Cross over without fail, or the king and all the people with him will be wiped out.’” Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A servant girl would go and pass the news to them, and they would go and tell King David, because they could not risk being seen entering the city. But a young man spotted them and told Absalom. So the two hurried off to Bahurim, to the house of a man whose courtyard had a well, and they climbed down into it. The woman of the house took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain on it, so that nothing could be seen. Absalom’s servants came to the house and asked the woman, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” The woman told them, “They have gone across the stream.” They searched but could not find them, so they went back to Jerusalem.

After the men had left, the two climbed out of the well and went to tell King David. They said to David, “Get up and cross the water at once, for this is what Ahithophel has advised against you.” So David and all the people with him set out and crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not a single one was left who had not crossed the Jordan. Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been carried out. He saddled his donkey and set off for home, to his own town. He put his household in order and then hanged himself. So he died, and they buried him in his father’s tomb.

David at Mahanaim

David had reached Mahanaim by the time Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel. Absalom had put Amasa in command of the army instead of Joab. Amasa’s father was a man named Ithra the Israelite, who had slept with Abigail daughter of Nahash, the sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother. Israel and Absalom made camp in the land of Gilead.

When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim brought bedding, basins and clay pots, and wheat and barley, flour and roasted grain, beans and lentils, honey and curds, sheep, and cheese from the herd, as food for David and the people with him. They said, “The people have become hungry and tired and thirsty in the wilderness.”

fields.title: 2 Samuel 18
fields.body_html:
Absalom is defeated and killed

David counted the troops who were with him and appointed commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds over them. Then David sent the troops out in three divisions: one under Joab’s command, one under Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and one under Ittai the Gittite. The king told the troops, “I am going out with you myself.” But the troops said, “You must not go out. If we have to run, they will not care about us. Even if half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth 10,000 of us. So it is better for you to help us from the city.”

The king answered them, “I will do whatever you think best.” So the king stood beside the gate while all the troops marched out in units of hundreds and of thousands. The king gave an order to Joab, Abishai and Ittai: “For my sake, deal gently with the young man Absalom.” All the troops heard the king give this order about Absalom to all the commanders. The army marched out into the open country to face Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim. There the army of Israel was defeated by David’s men, and the slaughter there that day was great: 20,000 men. The fighting spread out over the whole countryside, and the forest claimed more lives that day than the sword did. Absalom happened to come upon some of David’s men. He was riding his mule, and when it passed beneath the tangled branches of a great terebinth, Absalom’s head was caught fast in the tree. He was left hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him kept going. One man saw it and told Joab, “I have just seen Absalom hanging in a terebinth!” Joab said to the man who had told him, “You saw him? Then why did you not strike him down to the ground right there? I would have given you about 4 ounces of silver and a belt.” But the man answered Joab, “Even if I felt the weight of about 25 pounds of silver in my hands, I would not raise my hand against the king’s son. We all heard the king command you and Abishai and Ittai, ‘Whoever you are, keep the young man Absalom safe.’ And if I had acted treacherously and put my own life at risk, you yourself would have stood back and kept out of it, because nothing is hidden from the king.” Joab said, “I will not waste any more time with you like this.” He took three rods in his hand and drove them into Absalom’s chest while Absalom was still alive in the middle of the tree. Then ten young men, Joab’s armor-bearers, closed in around Absalom, struck him down and killed him. Then Joab sounded the trumpet, and the troops turned back from chasing Israel, because Joab held the army back. They took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest, then raised a huge heap of stones over him. And all Israel fled, every man to his home.

During his lifetime Absalom had taken a pillar and set it up for himself in the King’s Valley, because he said, “I have no son to keep my name remembered.” He named the pillar after himself, and it is called Absalom’s Monument to this day.

David hears the news

Then Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, “Let me run and take the news to the king that the LORD has vindicated him by rescuing him from his enemies.” But Joab told him, “You are not the one to carry the news today. You may carry news another day, but not today, because the king’s son is dead.” Then Joab said to the Cushite, “Go and tell the king what you have seen.” The Cushite bowed down to Joab and ran off. Ahimaaz son of Zadok spoke to Joab again. “Whatever happens,” he said, “please let me run after the Cushite too.” Joab replied, “Why would you want to run, my son? You have no news that will bring you any reward.” “Whatever happens,” Ahimaaz said, “I want to run.” “Then run,” Joab told him. So Ahimaaz ran by the road through the plain and got ahead of the Cushite. David was sitting between the inner and outer gates. The watchman went up to the roof over the gate, on the wall. He looked out and saw a man running alone. The watchman called down and told the king. The king said, “If he is alone, he is bringing news.” The man came closer and closer. Then the watchman saw another man running, and he called down to the gatekeeper, “Look, there is a man running alone!” The king said, “He is bringing news too.” The watchman said, “It looks to me as if the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok.” “He is a good man,” the king said. “He is coming with good news.” Ahimaaz called out to the king, “All is well!” He bowed down before the king with his face to the ground and said, “Blessed be the LORD your God, who has handed over the men who raised their hands against my lord the king!” The king asked, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” Ahimaaz answered, “I saw a great commotion just as Joab was sending the king’s servant and your servant, but I do not know what it was about.” The king said, “Step aside and stand here.” So he stepped aside and stood there. Just then the Cushite arrived, and he said, “Good news for my lord the king! Today the LORD has vindicated you by rescuing you from all who rose up against you.”

The king asked the Cushite, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” The Cushite replied, “May all your enemies, my lord the king, and all who rise up to harm you, end up like that young man!”

The king was shaken. He went up to the room over the gate and wept, and as he went, these were his words: “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I could have died in your place, Absalom, my son, my son!”

fields.title: 2 Samuel 19
fields.body_html:
David mourns for Absalom

Joab was told, “The king is weeping and mourning for Absalom.” So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the troops, because the troops heard it said that day, “The king is grieving over his son.” That day the troops slipped quietly into the city, the way troops creep in when they are ashamed because they have fled from battle. The king covered his face and cried out in a loud voice, “My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!”

Then Joab went in to the king in the house and said, “You have today disgraced all your servants, who this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters, your wives and your concubines, because you show love to those who hate you and hatred to those who love you. Today you have shown that your commanders and servants count for nothing with you. I know now that if all of us had died today and Absalom were alive, you would think it right. So now get up, go out and speak to the hearts of your servants. By the LORD I swear: unless you go out, not a single man will spend this night with you. That would be a worse disaster for you than any that has come on you since you were young.”

So the king got up and took his seat in the gate. All the troops were told, “The king is sitting in the gate,” and they all came into his presence. As for Israel, they had fled, each man to his home.

David returns to Jerusalem

Throughout all the tribes of Israel the people were arguing with one another. “The king rescued us from the power of our enemies,” they said. “He saved us from the power of the Philistines. Yet now he has fled out of the land because of Absalom. And Absalom, whom we anointed to rule over us, has died in battle. So now, why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?”

King David sent this message to the priests Zadok and Abiathar: “Ask the elders of Judah, ‘Why should you be last of all in bringing the king back to his palace? What all Israel is saying has reached the king in his house. You are my brothers; you are my own bone and flesh. Why then should you be last of all in bringing the king back?’ And say to Amasa, ‘Are you not my own bone and flesh? May God deal with me ever so severely if you do not become commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.’” So he won over the hearts of all the men of Judah as if they were one man, and they sent word to the king: “Come back, you and all your officials.” So the king started back and came as far as the Jordan. Judah had come to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring him across the Jordan. Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, came down in haste with the men of Judah to meet King David. With him were a thousand men from Benjamin, and Ziba the attendant of Saul’s household, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants. They rushed down to the Jordan ahead of the king. They kept crossing back and forth at the ford to bring the king’s household over and to do whatever he wished. As the king was about to cross the Jordan, Shimei son of Gera fell down before him. He said to the king, “May my lord not hold me guilty. Do not remember the wrong your servant did on the day my lord the king went out from Jerusalem. Let the king put it out of his mind. Your servant knows that I have sinned. But see, today I have come, the first of all the house of Joseph, to come down and meet my lord the king.”

Abishai son of Zeruiah spoke up and said, “Should not Shimei be put to death for this? He cursed the LORD’s anointed!”

David said, “Sons of Zeruiah, what business is this of yours? Why should you set yourselves against me today? Is anyone in Israel to be put to death on this day? Do I not know that today I am king over Israel?” So the king said to Shimei, “You will not die.” And the king gave him his oath.

Mephibosheth, Saul’s grandson, also came down to meet the king. From the day the king left until the day he returned safely, he had not tended his feet, trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes. When he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, the king asked him, “Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?” He answered, “My lord the king, my servant deceived me. Your servant said, ‘I will have the donkey saddled for myself so that I can ride it and go with the king,’ since your servant is lame. He has told my lord the king lies about your servant. Yet my lord the king is like an angel of God, so do whatever seems good to you. My father’s whole house deserved nothing but death from my lord the king, yet you gave your servant a place among those who eat at your table. So what right do I have to make any more appeals to the king?”

The king said to him, “Why say any more about your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba are to divide the land.” Mephibosheth said to the king, “Let him take it all, now that my lord the king has come home safely.”

David and Barzillai

Barzillai the Gileadite had also come down from Rogelim, and he crossed the Jordan with the king to see him on his way across the river. Barzillai was very old, eighty years of age. He had supplied the king’s needs while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man. The king said to Barzillai, “Come across with me, and I will provide for you in Jerusalem, at my side.” But Barzillai answered the king, “How many years do I have left to live, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king? I am eighty years old today. Can I still tell what is pleasant from what is not? Can your servant taste what I eat and drink? Do I still hear the voices of men and women singing? Why should your servant be one more burden to my lord the king? Your servant will go only a short way across the Jordan with the king. Why should the king give me a reward like this? Please let your servant go back, so that I may die in my own town near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him cross the river with my lord the king, and treat him in whatever way seems good to you.”

The king answered, “Chimham will cross with me, and I myself will do for him whatever you think good. And anything you ask of me, I will do for you.” So all the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed too. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai went back to his home.

Israel and Judah quarrel

The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went with him. All the people of Judah had brought the king across, and half the people of Israel as well. Just then the men of Israel all came to the king and said to him, “Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away? Why did they take the king and his household over the Jordan, along with all David’s men?”

All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, “We did it because the king is our close relative. Why are you so angry about this? Have we eaten anything at the king’s expense? Have we been given any gift?”

The men of Israel replied to the men of Judah, “Ten shares in the king are ours, and in David too our share is larger than yours. So why do you treat us as if we did not matter? Was it not we who first said that our king should be brought back?” But the men of Judah answered more fiercely than the men of Israel.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 20
fields.body_html:
Sheba’s revolt

Now a worthless man named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite, happened to be there. He blew the trumpet and cried out, “We have no part in David, no inheritance in Jesse’s son! Each man to his tents, Israel!” So all the men of Israel deserted David and followed Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah kept close to their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem. When David came back to his palace in Jerusalem, the king took the ten concubines he had left to look after the palace and placed them under guard in a house. He supplied their needs, but he did not sleep with them. They were kept shut away until the day they died, living as widows while their husband was alive.

The king told Amasa, “Call up the men of Judah and have them with me within three days, and be here yourself.” Amasa went to call up Judah, but he was delayed past the time the king had set for him.

David said to Abishai, “Sheba son of Bichri will now hurt us worse than Absalom did. Take your lord’s servants and go after him, or he will find fortified cities for himself and slip out of our sight.” So Joab’s men went out after Abishai, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites and all the warriors. They marched out of Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri. When they were at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was dressed in his soldier’s tunic, and over it he wore a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened at his waist. As he stepped forward, the sword fell out.

Joab kills Amasa

Joab said to Amasa, “Are you well, my brother?” Then with his right hand Joab took hold of Amasa’s beard to kiss him. Amasa was not on guard against the sword in Joab’s hand, and Joab stabbed him in the stomach with it and spilled his insides on the ground. He did not have to strike him a second time, and Amasa died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai went on in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri. One of Joab’s young men stood beside Amasa’s body and said, “Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is on David’s side, follow Joab!” Amasa lay in a pool of his own blood in the middle of the road. When the man saw that all the troops were stopping, he dragged Amasa off the road into a field and threw a cloak over him, because he saw that everyone who came by him stopped. Once Amasa had been moved off the road, all the men went on after Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri. Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel as far as Abel Beth-maacah. All the Berites gathered and followed him there as well. Joab’s forces came and besieged Sheba in Abel Beth-maacah. They piled up a siege ramp against the city, and it stood against the outer rampart. All the troops with Joab were battering the wall to bring it down. Then a wise woman in the city called out, “Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, please, ‘Come over here so I can speak with you.’” He came near to her, and the woman asked, “Are you Joab?” “I am,” he answered. She said to him, “Listen to what your servant has to say.” “I am listening,” he replied. She went on, “Long ago people used to say, ‘Go and ask in Abel,’ and that is how they settled things. I am one of the peaceable and faithful in Israel. You are out to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why should you swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?”

Joab answered, “Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy! That is not how it is. A man from the hill country of Ephraim named Sheba son of Bichri has raised his hand against the king, against David. Hand him over, him alone, and I will withdraw from the city.” The woman said to Joab, “You will see: his head will be thrown to you over the wall.” Then the woman went to all the people with her wise advice, and they beheaded Sheba son of Bichri and tossed his head out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and his men left the city and scattered, each to his home. And Joab went back to the king in Jerusalem.

David’s officials

Joab was commander of all Israel’s army; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; Adoram was over the forced labor; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder; Sheva was secretary; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; and Ira the Jairite was also David’s priest.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 21
fields.body_html:
The Gibeonites are avenged

In the days of David there was a famine for three years in a row, so David sought the presence of the LORD. The LORD said, “It is because of Saul and his bloodstained house, because he put the Gibeonites to death.” So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (The Gibeonites were not Israelites; they were what was left of the Amorites. The Israelites had sworn an oath to them, but in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah, Saul had tried to wipe them out.) David asked the Gibeonites, “What should I do for you? How can I make atonement, so that you will bless the inheritance of the LORD?” The Gibeonites answered him, “Our claim against Saul and his family is not a matter of silver or gold, and it is not our right to put anyone in Israel to death.” David said, “Then what are you asking me to do for you?” They said to the king, “As for the man who nearly wiped us out and plotted against us, so that we have no place left anywhere in the territory of Israel, let seven of his male descendants be handed over to us, and we will impale them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the one the LORD chose.” The king said, “I will hand them over.” But the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, because of the oath before the LORD that bound David and Saul’s son Jonathan to each other. Instead the king took the two sons Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, together with the five sons Saul’s daughter Michal had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai of Meholah. He handed them over to the Gibeonites, who impaled them on the mountain before the LORD. All seven of them died together. They were put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest. Then Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and laid it out on the rock as a place for herself. From the beginning of the harvest until rain fell on the bodies from the sky, she did not let the birds come down on them by day or the wild animals by night. Word reached David of what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul’s concubine, had done. David went and took the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan from the leading men of Jabesh-gilead. They had carried them off secretly from the open square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them up on the day they struck Saul down on Gilboa. He brought up from there the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan, and the bones of the men who had been impaled were gathered too. They buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the tomb of Kish, Saul’s father, at Zela in the territory of Benjamin. They did everything the king commanded, and after that God answered prayer for the land.

Battles with the Philistines

Once again there was war between the Philistines and Israel. David went down with his men, and they fought against the Philistines, and David grew exhausted. Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the Rapha, whose bronze spear weighed about 7 1/2 pounds, and who was armed with a new weapon, meant to kill David. But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David’s help. He struck down the Philistine and killed him. Then David’s men took an oath before him: “Never again will you go out with us to battle. You must not let the lamp of Israel be put out.”

After this there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob. That was when Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, one of the descendants of the Rapha.

There was another battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim, from Bethlehem, killed Goliath of Gath, whose spear had a shaft like a weaver’s beam.

There was another battle at Gath, where there was a man of great size who had six fingers on each of his hands and six toes on each of his feet, twenty-four altogether. He also was descended from the Rapha. When he taunted Israel, Jonathan son of Shimeah, David’s brother, killed him. These four were descendants of the Rapha in Gath, and they fell at the hands of David and his men.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 22
fields.body_html:
David’s song of praise

David sang the words of this song to the LORD on the day the LORD rescued him from the power of all his enemies and from the power of Saul. He said: “The LORD is my cliff, my stronghold, the one who sets me free, my God, my rock, in whom I shelter, my shield, my strong salvation, my tower on the heights and my place of escape, my savior; you save me from violence. I call on the LORD, who is worthy of praise, and from my enemies I am rescued. For the waves of death swirled around me; floods of ruin overwhelmed me with terror. The ropes of Sheol coiled around me; death’s traps lay right in front of me. When I was hard pressed I called on the LORD; I called to my God. Out of his temple he listened to my voice; my cry reached his ears. Then the earth shuddered and rocked; the foundations of the heavens trembled and were shaken, because he was furious. Smoke rose from his nostrils, and fire that consumes came from his mouth; burning coals flamed out of it. He bowed the heavens low and came down; storm clouds were dark beneath his feet. Riding on a cherub, he flew; he appeared on the wings of the wind. He made darkness a tent all around him, a mass of rain clouds, thick clouds of the sky. Out of the brightness in front of him burning coals flamed up. The LORD thundered from heaven; the Most High raised his voice. He let arrows fly and scattered the enemy; he sent lightning and threw them into confusion. The beds of the sea came into view; the world’s foundations lay bare at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of breath from his nostrils. From on high he stretched out his hand and seized me; he pulled me out of deep waters. He snatched me away from my powerful enemy, from those who hated me, because they were stronger than I was. They came at me on my day of disaster, but the LORD held me up. He led me out into open country; he set me free, because he was pleased with me. The LORD treated me as my right conduct deserved; he rewarded me because my hands were clean. For I have walked in the LORD’s ways and have not turned from my God to do evil. All his rulings have been in front of me; I have not turned aside from his laws. I was whole-hearted toward him; I guarded myself from sin. So the LORD rewarded me for doing right, for the cleanness he could see in me. To the faithful you are faithful; to the strong who have integrity you show integrity. To the pure you prove yourself pure, but with the crooked you are subtle. You rescue people who are humbled, but your eyes are on the proud, and you bring them down. You are my lamp, LORD; the LORD brightens my darkness. With you I can rush an armed band; by the strength of my God I can vault a wall. This is God: his way is without flaw; the word of the LORD is tested and true; he is a shield for all who make him their refuge. Is there any God but the LORD? Is there any rock but our God? the God who is my strong fortress, who sets my way free and makes it secure, who makes my feet as sure as a deer’s and sets me firm on the heights, who trains my hands for war, so that my arms can draw a bronze bow. You have handed me your saving shield, and your answer has made me great. You make room for my steps, so my ankles do not turn. I chased my enemies and wiped them out; I did not give up the chase until I had made an end of them. I made an end of them and shattered them, and they did not stand again; they lay fallen at my feet. You strapped strength on me for the fight; you brought my attackers to their knees beneath me. You put my enemies to flight before me, and I destroyed those who hated me. They looked for help, but no one came to save them; they looked to the LORD, but he gave them no answer. I ground them as fine as the dust of the ground; I crushed them and trampled them like mud in the streets. You set me free from the quarrels of my own people; you kept me at the head of the nations. A nation I never knew now serves me. Foreigners come to me cringing; the moment they hear, they obey me. Foreigners lose heart; they put on their belts and come out of their fortresses. The LORD is alive! Blessed be my rock! May God, the rock who saves me, be lifted high, the God who avenges me and brings nations down beneath me, who brings me out from among my enemies. You raise me high above my attackers; you save me from the violent man. That is why I will give you thanks, LORD, among the nations, and sing praise to your name. He is a tower of victories for his king; he keeps faith in loyal love with his anointed one, with David and his line for all time.”

fields.title: 2 Samuel 23
fields.body_html:
David’s last words

These are the final words of David: the oracle of Jesse’s son David, the oracle of the man who was raised on high, the one anointed by the God of Jacob, the sweet singer of Israel’s songs. The Spirit of the LORD has spoken through me; his word is on my tongue. The God of Israel has spoken; the Rock of Israel said to me: “One who rules over people in righteousness, who rules in the fear of God, is like the morning light when the sun rises, a morning without clouds, like the brightness after rain that brings the grass out of the earth.” Is not my house like this with God? For he has made an everlasting covenant with me, set in order in every part and secured. All my salvation and all my desire, will he not make them grow? But the worthless are all like thorns that are tossed aside, for no one picks them up by hand. Whoever touches them must be armed with iron or the shaft of a spear, and they are burned up completely with fire where they lie.

David’s mighty warriors

These are the names of David’s mighty warriors. Josheb-Basshebeth the Tahchemonite was chief of the officers. He was also called Adino the Eznite, and he killed eight hundred men at one time.

Next to him was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite. He was one of the three mighty warriors with David when they defied the Philistines who had gathered there for battle, and the men of Israel withdrew. He stood his ground and struck down Philistines until his hand grew tired and stuck fast to his sword. On that day the LORD won a great victory, and the troops came back to him only to strip the dead.

Next to him was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines had massed in a troop where a plot of land was full of lentils, and the troops ran from the Philistines. But he took his stand in the middle of the plot, defended it and struck down the Philistines, and the LORD won a great victory.

Once, at harvest time, three chief men of the Thirty went down and joined David at the cave of Adullam, while a band of Philistines was camped in the Valley of Rephaim. At that time David was in the stronghold, and a Philistine garrison was then in Bethlehem. David had a longing and said, “If only someone would get me water to drink from Bethlehem’s well, the one by the gate!” So the three mighty warriors broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate, and carried it back to David. But he would not drink it. Instead he poured it out as an offering to the LORD. He said, “The LORD, far be it from me to do this! Is it not the blood of men who went at the risk of their lives?” So he would not drink it. Such were the deeds of the three mighty warriors.

Abishai, the brother of Joab son of Zeruiah, was chief of the Three. He raised his spear against three hundred men and killed them, and he won a name alongside the Three. Was he not honored above the Three? He became their commander, but he did not reach the rank of the Three.

Benaiah son of Jehoiada was the son of a brave man from Kabzeel who did great deeds. He struck down the two champions of Moab. He also went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion. He also struck down an Egyptian, an impressive-looking man. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down against him with a club, snatched the spear from the Egyptian’s grip and killed him with his own weapon. Such were the deeds of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he won a name alongside the three mighty warriors. He was honored above the Thirty, but he did not reach the rank of the Three. And David put him in charge of his bodyguard.

The Thirty

Among the Thirty were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan son of Dodo from Bethlehem, Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite,

Helez the Paltite, Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite,

Abiezer the Anathothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite,

Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite,

Heleb son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ittai son of Ribai from Gibeah of the Benjaminites,

Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hiddai from the ravines of Gaash,

Abi-Albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite,

Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,

Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite,

Eliphelet son of Ahasbai the Maacathite, Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,

Hezrai the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite,

Igal son of Nathan from Zobah, Bani the Gadite,

Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah,

Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,

and Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.

fields.title: 2 Samuel 24
fields.body_html:
David counts the people

Once more the anger of the LORD flared up against Israel, and he stirred David up against them, saying, “Go and count Israel and Judah.” So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army who was with him, “Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and register the people, so that I may know how many there are.”

But Joab said to the king, “May the LORD your God make the people a hundred times as many as they are, and may my lord the king see it with his own eyes! But why does my lord the king want to do this?” But the king’s order overruled Joab and the army commanders, so Joab and the commanders of the army left the king’s presence to register the people of Israel. They crossed the Jordan and camped at Aroer, on the south side of the town in the middle of the valley; then they went through Gad and on to Jazer. Then they went to Gilead and the land of Tahtim-hodshi, came on to Dan-jaan, and went around toward Sidon. They came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the towns of the Hivites and Canaanites, and then went out to the Negev of Judah, at Beersheba. When they had gone through the whole land, they came back to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days. Joab gave the king the total of the people who had been registered: in Israel there were 800,000 able-bodied men who could handle a sword, and in Judah 500,000. But after David had counted the people, his conscience struck him. David said to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly by doing this. Now, LORD, please take away your servant’s guilt, for I have acted very foolishly.” When David got up in the morning, the word of the LORD had come to the prophet Gad, David’s seer: “Go and tell David, ‘The LORD says this: I am setting three things before you. Choose one of them, and I will do it to you.’” So Gad went to David and told him, “Shall seven years of famine come on your land? Or three months of running from your enemies while they chase you? Or three days of plague in your land? Now think it over and decide what answer I should take back to the one who sent me.”

David said to Gad, “I am in deep distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great; but do not let me fall into human hands.” So the LORD sent a plague on Israel from that morning until the time that had been set, and 70,000 of the people died, from Dan to Beersheba. But as the angel reached out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented from the disaster. He said to the angel who was bringing destruction on the people, “Enough! Now hold back your hand.” The angel of the LORD was then by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel who was striking down the people, he said to the LORD, “I am the one who has sinned; I am the one who has done wrong. But what have these sheep done? Please let your hand be against me and my father’s family.”

David builds an altar

That same day Gad came to David and told him, “Go up and set up an altar for the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” So David went up as Gad had told him, just as the LORD had commanded. When Araunah looked down and saw the king and his officials coming toward him, he went out and bowed before the king with his face to the ground. Araunah asked, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David answered, “To buy your threshing floor, so that I can build an altar to the LORD and the plague on the people may be stopped.” Araunah said to David, “Let my lord the king take whatever he thinks best and offer it up. Look, here are the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the oxen’s yokes for the wood. All this, my king, Araunah gives to the king.” And Araunah said to the king, “May the LORD your God accept you.” But the king said to Araunah, “No, I insist on paying you a price for it. I will not offer the LORD my God burnt offerings at no cost to myself.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for about 1 1/4 pounds of silver. David built an altar to the LORD there and sacrificed burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered the prayers for the land, and the plague on Israel was stopped.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
David built an altar to the LORD there and sacrificed burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered the prayers for the land, and the plague on Israel was stopped.

— 2 Samuel 24:25

2 Samuel ends at an altar. The king who had danced before the ark, sinned with Bathsheba, wept on the Mount of Olives and cried out for Absalom, stands at last on a threshing floor outside Jerusalem, having confessed one more sin, and offers sacrifices he has paid for himself. The angel’s hand is held back. The plague stops. It is a quiet ending for Israel’s greatest king: an old man praying for his people, and the mercy of God answering.

The question the book leaves with you

The book has told us two things about David, and it insists that both are true. God made him an everlasting promise: his house, his kingdom and his throne would stand firm forever. And David failed, badly, in ways that wounded his family and his nation for the rest of his life. The sword never did depart from his house.

That is the question 2 Samuel leaves with every reader: can the promises of God survive the sins of the people he makes them to? The book’s answer is yes, but not cheaply. David was forgiven the moment he said “I have sinned against the LORD”, and he still lost the child, and Amnon, and Absalom. Grace did not cancel the consequences. But neither did the consequences cancel the grace. God had said that he would discipline David’s son “with a rod such as people use”, and that his faithful love would not be taken away, and he did not take back his word.

David’s own last words hold the two together. He sings of the righteous ruler who is like “a morning without clouds”, and then asks a question about his own house, and answers it with the covenant:

Is not my house like this with God? For he has made an everlasting covenant with me, set in order in every part and secured. All my salvation and all my desire, will he not make them grow?

— 2 Samuel 23:5

His hope at the end of his life is not in himself, or his sons, or his kingdom. It is in a covenant God made and God will keep.

Where the story goes next

The story continues without a break into 1 Kings, which opens with David old and cold in his bed, and a struggle over who will succeed him. Solomon builds the temple. But the kingdom divides after Solomon’s death, and Kings ends with Jerusalem destroyed and David’s heir an exile in Babylon. The prophets go on looking, through all of it, for a son of David who will reign in righteousness, on whom the Spirit of the LORD will rest.

The New Testament opens with that hope fulfilled. Its first verse calls Jesus “the son of David, the son of Abraham”. He is born in Bethlehem, “David’s town”. And at its very end, the risen Christ gives himself the title that gathers up the whole of 2 Samuel, the promise to David’s house and the morning without clouds:

“I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright morning star.”

— Revelation 22:16

Where to go from here

David’s story has been preached, prayed and sung in the church for as long as there has been a church, and some of the best of that work is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the whole book. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles: The Kingdom Under David” reads David’s reign as a picture of the kingdom of God under the king of his own choosing.
  • On the promise to David (2 Samuel 7). Book XVII of Augustine’s The City of God, which argues that the promises Nathan brought to David are not fulfilled in Solomon but in Christ.
  • On David’s sin and repentance (2 Samuel 11–12). “A Pure Heart”, on Psalm 51 and Nathan’s rebuke, in The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original; E. M. Bounds’s Prayer and Praying Men, whose chapter “Praying Saints of the Old Testaments (Continued)” follows David’s prayer for the dying child and his confession to Nathan; and the eighteenth chapter of Clement of Rome’s The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, “David as an example of humility”, on Psalm 51.
  • On David’s last words (2 Samuel 23). J. C. Ryle’s sermon Without Clouds (2 Samuel 23:4–5), on the old king’s sorrow over his house and his comfort in the everlasting covenant.
  • On David and the Spirit. A. B. Simpson’s chapter “The Holy Spirit in the Lives of Saul and David”, in The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High.
  • For reading with children. “A Seat at the King’s Table”, on David and Mephibosheth, and “The Story of the Little Lamb”, on Nathan’s parable, in Tell Me the Story – Book 3: Kings and Prophets; and “A House Forever”, on 2 Samuel 7 and 11–12, in The Big Story, both Ochorus Originals.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 2 Samuel in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read the Psalms that bear David’s name, beginning with the song this book itself records, almost word for word, as Psalm 18. They are the inside of the story 2 Samuel tells from outside: the prayers of a king who knew where his help came from.

He said: “The LORD is my cliff, my stronghold, the one who sets me free,

— 2 Samuel 22:2
